name: Amalek
title: Ancestor of the Amalekites
summary: Amalek was the son of Eliphaz and his Horite concubine Timna, and thus the grandson of Esau. He was counted as a tribal chief in Edom and is known as the ancestor of the Amalekites – a nomadic desert people who throughout biblical history represented a persistent and particularly serious hostile threat to Israel. When the Amalekites attacked the Israelites from behind at Rephidim, striking among the weakest, shortly after their deliverance from Egypt, it led to an extraordinary divine declaration of war against Amalek from generation to generation and that their memory should be blotted out. Through the period of the judges, Saul’s and David’s kingdoms, the Amalekites remained a recurring threat. Saul’s disobedience to the divine command to carry out judgment on them cost him his kingship, and David himself had to fight them at Ziklag. Theologically, the line from Amalek extends all the way to the book of Esther, where Haman the Agagite – with roots in the royal lineage of the Amalekites – sought to destroy the Jewish people, but ultimately perished himself. Thus, Amalek stands in the biblical narrative as a consistent warning against hostility toward God’s people and about God’s final judgment on such resistance.

keyEvents.title: The Birth and Lineage of Amalek
keyEvents.description: Amalek was born as the son of Eliphaz (Esau's son) and his concubine Timna. He is counted among Esau's descendants and became a tribal chief in Edom.

keyEvents.title: The Attack of the Amalekites on Israel at Rephidim
keyEvents.description: The Amalekites, descendants of Amalek, attacked the Israelites shortly after leaving Egypt at Rephidim. Moses held up his hands while Joshua fought and defeated them.

keyEvents.title: God's Declaration of Eternal War Against Amalek
keyEvents.description: After the victory at Rephidim, the Lord declared that He would wage war against Amalek from generation to generation, and that the memory of Amalek should be blotted out under heaven.

keyEvents.title: The Command to Remember What Amalek Did
keyEvents.description: Moses reminded the people how the Amalekites cowardly attacked the weakest and most exhausted at the rear of the caravan, and commanded Israel to blot out the memory of Amalek when they found rest in the land.

keyEvents.title: Saul and God's Judgment on the Amalekites
keyEvents.description: God commanded King Saul through the prophet Samuel to completely destroy the Amalekites as punishment for what they had done to Israel. Saul won, but spared King Agag and the best of the livestock, which led God to reject him as king.

keyEvents.title: David's Battle Against the Amalekites at Ziklag
keyEvents.description: The Amalekites plundered and burned Ziklag and took David's family and the families of his men captive. David pursued them, defeated them, and rescued everyone.

versions.summary: Amalek was the grandson of Esau and the ancestor of the Amalekites, a people who became Israel's archenemy throughout much of the Old Testament. The Amalekites attacked Israel repeatedly, and God declared eternal war against them. The name Amalek became synonymous with hostility toward God's people.
versions.title: Ancestor of the Amalekites
versions.reason: [minor] The role 'warrior' is not directly attested for the person Amalek himself in the Bible. It is his descendants, the Amalekites, who are known as warriors. Amalek himself is primarily known as a forefather. The role 'forefather' would be more precise than 'patriarch', and 'warrior' should be removed or replaced with 'tribal chief' based on Genesis 36:16 where he is called a tribal chief.; [major] According to Genesis 36:11-12, Amalek's half-brothers (Eliphaz's sons by his wife) were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam and Kenaz. But Amalek was the son of the concubine Timna, so he is a half-brother, not a full brother. Nevertheless, the list is correct as siblings (half-brothers). However, 'Zepho' should be checked – in some texts it reads 'Zepho' (Genesis 36:11) or 'Zephi' (1 Chronicles 1:36). The form 'Zepho' is acceptable.; [minor] The last four events (Rephidim, eternal war, the Deuteronomy command, Saul's battle, David's battle) concern the Amalekites as a people, not the person Amalek himself. It is still reasonable to include them to show Amalek's legacy and significance, but it should be reflected more clearly in the descriptions that this concerns his descendants.; [minor] The event concerning Saul and the Amalekites covers a wide range of verses. It may be useful to also include verses 22-23, where Samuel confronts Saul with his disobedience, but this is an editorial consideration.; [minor] The summary is good, but could clarify that Amalek was the son of Eliphaz's concubine Timna, which provides important context about his position in the family line.; [major] Footnotes are missing. There are several interesting historical, linguistic and theological aspects concerning Amalek that should be covered, including the rabbinic tradition about Amalek, its typological significance, and the connection to Haman in the book of Esther.

versions.summary: Amalek was the grandson of Esau, born as the son of Eliphaz and his concubine Timna. He is counted among Esau's descendants in Edom and became the ancestor of the Amalekites, a nomadic desert people who were Israel's archenemy through much of the Old Testament. The Amalekites attacked Israel repeatedly – first at Rephidim shortly after leaving Egypt, and later in numerous conflicts during the period of the judges and the monarchy. God declared eternal war against Amalek and commanded that their memory be blotted out. The name Amalek became a lasting symbol of hostility toward God's people, a line extending all the way to Haman the Agagite in the book of Esther.

It should be 'horittisk' with Latin letters.; [minor] The event concerning David's battle at Ziklag refers to 1 Sam 30, which is bookId 9. This is correct. versions.summary: Amalek was a descendant of Esau through his father Eliphaz, born to the concubine Timna, who had Horite origins. As a tribal chief in Edom, he became the ancestor of the Amalekites – a nomadic desert people who in biblical history stand as the very archetype of hostility toward Israel. Already at Rephidim, shortly after the deliverance from Egypt, the Amalekites attacked the Israelites from behind, targeting those who were weakest. This event led to God’s unique declaration of eternal war against Amalek, a judgment that echoes throughout the Old Testament. From the time of the judges through the reigns of Saul and David, the Amalekites remained a recurring threat. Saul’s failure to carry out God’s judgment against them cost him his kingship. The theological line from Amalek extends all the way to the book of Esther, where Haman the Agagite – linked to the royal lineage of the Amalekites – threatened to destroy the Jewish people, only to be overcome himself.
versions.title: Ancestor of the Amalekites
versions.reason: [minor] Sefo is a variant of the name, but the most common form in Norwegian Bible translations is 'Sfo' or 'Sefo'. More importantly: According to Genesis 36:11–12, Amalek's half-siblings (Eliphaz's sons by his primary wife) are Teman, Omar, Sefo, Gatam, and Kenaz. This is correct. However, it should be clarified that these are half-siblings, not full siblings, since Amalek was born of the concubine Timna, while the others were born of Eliphaz's primary wife. The list is nevertheless accurate as a sibling listing.; [minor] The event 'David's battle against the Amalekites at Ziklag' refers to 1 Samuel 30 (bookId 9), which is correct. But it may be noted that this takes place in a book that, within the biblical canon, is counted as 1 Samuel.; [minor] The final footnote concerning the anachronism in Genesis 14:7 is categorized as 'theological', but it primarily concerns a literary/linguistic observation (proleptic use of a place name). The source type 'linguistic' would have been more precise.; [minor] The summary is very good, but the expression 'the very archetype of enmity toward Israel' is strong. Although this is theologically defensible, it could be nuanced somewhat to show that this is an interpretive tradition rather than an explicit biblical formulation. Nevertheless, the overall quality is high.

footnotes.text: In Talmudic and Midrashic literature (e.g., Sanhedrin 99b), there is a tradition that Timna first wished to convert to the faith of Abraham but was rejected by the patriarchs, and then became a concubine of Eliphaz. In this tradition, Amalek is understood as a result of that rejection—a warning about the consequences of turning away those who seek belonging among God's people.

The Amalekites operated mainly as a nomadic people in the Negev desert and the Sinai Peninsula. Egyptian texts from the New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BCE) mention restless nomadic groups in this area, referred to as 'shasu,' but it is debated whether any of these can be identified with the Amalekites.

Rabbinic tradition (Pesikta de-Rav Kahana) interprets the phrase 'from generation to generation' in Exodus 17:16 as a prophetic line extending from Amalek through Agag and onward to Haman—and sees the festival of Purim as the ultimate fulfillment of God's victory over Amalek's spiritual legacy.
